💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 03:48 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 07:04 EST, 19 November 2026.
  • The world has been waiting 13 years for GTA6 and footballers are not immune from the lure and addictive nature of the game.
  • In fact, top flight players are notorious gamers given their amount of free time after training and Bryan Mbeumo was one of many to share his excitement at the midnight release.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 03:48 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 07:04 EST, 19 November 2026.

The world has been waiting 13 years for GTA6 and footballers are not immune from the lure and addictive nature of the game.

In fact, top flight players are notorious gamers given their amount of free time after training and Bryan Mbeumo was one of many to share his excitement at the midnight release.

No doubt upcoming Man United boss Mauricio Pochettino would prefer his players to get a solid night's sleep ahead of taking his first training session on Thursday but Mbeumo couldn't resist a late-night session.

He shared the loading screen of the Rockstar game at midnight on his Instagram story with the word 'historic' as the clock ticked into Thursday morning.

It remains to be seen whether Mbeumo stayed up into the early hours playing but an estimated three million UK adults were expected to call in sick or take annual leave to play.

Sleep is vital for athletes to recover and perform at their best and one NBA star even predicted professionals across sports would see their output 'plummet' as a result of GTA's pull.

Bryan Mbeumo shared this picture on his Instagram story at midnight when GTA went live.

Mauricio Pochettino's first morning of training coincides with the release of GTA, played by Mbeumo and plenty of other athletes who looked forward to the late-night release.

Sources indicate that in a previous video clip online, Mbeumo was being interviewed while on his console and showed he'd pre-ordered the game, saying: 'I'm just waiting now, the game will make me stay at home every single day... after training.'.

Pochettino, who flew on a private jet to Manchester on Wednesday ahead of his first day in the job on Thursday, will no doubt have a keen eye on whether any of his stars are bleary-eyed in training.

The fresh boss has an incredibly tight turnaround to prepare for the huge clash with rivals Liverpool on Sunday at Anfield, but perhaps the Reds will also be dealing with GTA-mania.

Alexander Isak was asked about the game's release while on international duty with Sweden and admitted: 'Yeah, so I think it’ll be difficult to reach me from the 19th, when it comes out. I’ll be locked in. That’s the plan.'.

A renowned sleep coach for top athletes, Nick Littlehales, has opined on the effects late-night gaming can have.

'They get lost in it, it’s an engaging distraction, and it satisfies their competitive edge, but just like mindlessly scrolling YouTube or social media, you need to put your own filters and blockers in place, otherwise you’ll find yourself doing something ridiculously stupid and playing for hours and hours, hurting your performance,' he told Ozoon.

It has been revealed that 'We know it’s unrealistic to expect a player to just stop after exactly two hours when they’re in the zone. You have to accept it and ask them: "Are you prepared to sacrifice your nocturnal sleep to be awake and stimulated? Is it worth it?" If they insist on it, we look at scheduling it. Maybe they game late on Tuesdays, Thursdays.

In a recent development, 'You must have these open conversations instead of outright banning late-night gaming. If you just throw the book at them, they end up taking sleeping tablets, using snus, and taking unregulated supplements they don’t understand just so they can cope. When you help them manage their gaming, they usually start to self-regulate.'.

It’s safe to say Bryan Mbeumo is ready for GTA 6. 🤣🤣 pic.twitter.com/skkPM2GYo9.

Conor McGregor revealed that he would give employees at various businesses the day off.

People cheer as Grand Theft Auto VI goes live at London gaming venue XP Tavern.

Arsenal's Declan Rice could be another to be locked into the fresh GTA having previously spoken about how much gaming helps him switch off.

Industry observers note that he told GQ: 'I can never sleep after night games. It’s impossible. I’ll be that wired. I'll play Call of Duty, Grand Theft Auto, FIFA. Anything. Just play with a load of my friends. Adrenaline, everything. You don’t really settle down.

'I feel like when you’re playing at this level, your mind’s just constantly – it’s just going.'.

Football clubs, businesses and even schools are braced for the effects of the newly introduced game, with one head teacher in Chelmsford, Essex, entering students into a raffle to win a £10 Amazon voucher in an attempt to stop them bunking off.

UFC star Conor McGregor declared that he was giving the day off to 400 employees at his various businesses so they could play the game.

And Real Madrid goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois shared an image of himself playing the game, flying a helicopter after it was released.

The astonishing level of anticipation for GTA6 has banked more than £1.14bn in pre-orders alone and is set to become by far the highest grossing game ever made.

It debuted with a score of 99 on review aggregator website Metacritic – equalling 1998's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time as the highest-rated video game ever.

Some 2.8million UK adults are set to play the game on launch day alone, according to a Uswitch poll commissioned earlier this month.

Over in the US, a number of athletes were frank in their honesty about how many of them would be addicted to the game.

Houston Rockets center Steven Adams previously said: 'You guys should anticipate November, the performance of the league, league-wide… GTA is dropping.

In a recent development, 'So look at NFL, look at all the leagues and watch them plummet, mate. Just for the month of November, performance is going to go down. It should come back up, though.

'Most of the boys will get it done, hopefully they finish the game. Coaching as well, by the way. The coaching and scouts are going to be horrendous, mate. Just for November, but it should bounce back in December, hopefully. Should be good.'.

🚨🇸🇪 Alexander Isak on the release of GTA 6: “Yeah, so I think it’ll be difficult to reach me from the 19th, when it comes out. I’ll be locked in. That’s the plan.” 😂 pic.twitter.com/LEhQQRo8pQ.

Real Madrid goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois shared this image from playing the game.

'I told my mom she might not hear from me for a couple of days,' Los Angeles Rams receiver Tutu Atwell, a Miami native, said with a grin. 'We've been waiting for this one for a long, long time, You know it's going to be a big one.'.

Plenty of other athletes share Atwell's excitement, but will prioritize their work on the field.

'I think a lot of athletes are responsible,' noted Los Angeles Rams offensive lineman Steve Avila. 'But if you could check guys' sleep scores … I think you'd see that some guys' hours are going to go way down, for sure.'.

Recent findings suggest that new York Jets running back Breece Hall concurs: 'Yeah, definitely getting the film done early, and then spending the extra hour or two on the game,' Hall said. 'But you've got to make sure you handle the main thing first before you have some fun.'.

There were some technological concerns in the hours leading up to the game's release, with the official PlayStation Network status website yesterday acknowledging some players were unable to access online features.

A statement on the website read: 'You might have difficulty launching games, apps, or network features. We're working to resolve the concern as soon as possible. Thank you for your patience.'.

Declan Rice is another star to stay up late gaming as it helps him switch off after big games.

Those issues appeared to be cleared up by midnight, with PlayStation declaring all of its services were 'up and running' in the hours after the game went live.

BT and EE called the upcoming launch an 'unprecedented gaming download event' because of the size of the game and the number of people expected to play.

The pre-download drove the second-highest broadband traffic peak ever on BT's networks, only beaten by Arsenal v Atletico Madrid in the Champions League in May, and Virgin Media O2 saw its highest-ever daily data volume last Tuesday.

While the exact number of people who have pre-ordered GTA VI is not known, Sony mentioned it is the most pre-ordered game in the history of PlayStation Store.

Schools have urged pupils not to use the release of the game – which carries an age rating of 18 – as an excuse to skip lessons.

Sales of gaming consoles and accessories surged in the run-up to launch day.

A man walks past a Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI) digital billboard advert in Milan - the game's release has become a global event.

Department store chain John Lewis stated it had seen a 62 per cent year-on-year increase in sales of gaming consoles and accessories, while retailer Currys reported a 149 per cent increase in PlayStation 5 consoles alone.

GTA VI returns to the neon-soaked streets of Vice City, Rockstar's fictional version of Miami, which has featured in previous instalments of the series.

The game follows two protagonists, Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, who find themselves caught up in a criminal conspiracy in the fictional state of Leonida, inspired by Florida.

The pair become embroiled in a Bonnie and Clyde-style crime story after 'an easy score goes wrong', leaving them 'forced to rely on each other more than ever if they want to make it out alive'.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Koni De Winter spoke at an event at the AC Milan store today, and he covered numerous topics with a lot of openness.

It has been revealed that this season, De Winter has found himself in a upcoming, important light. Matteo Gabbia spent most of pre-season in the middle of the back three, but injuries have prevented him from playing much of a role in the campaign.

In a recent development, read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

According to recent reports, it’s an unfortunate shame and there may have been some worries about De Winter taking on this role. However, he’s taken the opportunity in his stride, looking every part a starter in Ruben Amorim’s defence.

According to recent reports, rumours about a fresh defender arriving will persist, so it’ll be interesting to see what happens with his minutes from January onwards. However, he’s created something of a headache, but it’s a good one to have.

Speaking to SportMediaset on the sidelines of the Meet&Greet at the Milan Store in San Babila, via MilanNews, De Winter looked at the rise in his playing time, Amorim’s closeness to the group and much more.

In a recent development, you also took over at Reggio Emilia when Gabbia was unfortunately injured. You’re practically always there; what does that mean to you?

It has been revealed that “I’m playing a lot, it’s great to be playing. We’re playing a lot, and these days you train more on taking care of your body, keeping healthy, and right now I’m doing that more, but it’s great to be playing a lot of games. Playing a lot of games for Milan, and it’s even better to win games.”.

It’s all great, but it wasn’t a given: you’ve earned this place as leader. Do you now feel like a leader of this AC Milan?

Sources indicate that “I feel good at this Milan club, and as I always say, I try to give what I can. It’s also true that I might have a more key position this year. That might be true, but I always try to do my part, give my all, and help my teammates.”.

Sources indicate that it’s clear, evident, that Amorim holds you in high regard, but what is Amorim like? An adjective.

Recent findings suggest that “I’d say he’s very human. He’s one of us, he laughs, he has fun, but when he has to be serious, he’s serious. He lives with the group, the group feels close to him, and I think that gives the players a good feeling. It’s nice to work for him and with him.”.

Is it true that he got very angry after the defeat against Ferencvaros?

“Yes, but I think the whole group felt that we had played a very poor game, so, as I saw it, my teammates saw it too.”.

Are Ferencvaros and Bologna two games you’re ready to say “never again” to? Will Frosinone be a different team?

“Yes, exactly, as I said, we are very confident, but sometimes even too much so, and then all matches are difficult against whoever we play against, and we have to understand this quickly and we can’t make the same mistakes.”.

Industry observers note that among the various critics, it’s remarked that this AC Milan team has enormous potential, but there are too many ups and downs. Does it need more consistency?

It has been revealed that “Yes, I think it hurts even more when we lose because we know we can do well, we can win every game. So yes, when we really lose, in the locker room you feel like we’ve let ourselves down first and then everyone else.”.

It has been revealed that you recently became the father of a beautiful baby girl. What are your nights like as a dad?

“At night, I’m fine. My girlfriend is working really hard, so it’s a lot for me. I mean, I get up sometimes, but it’s much quieter. I think it’s harder for her.”.

And how much has life changed with the arrival of a daughter?

It has been revealed that “It’s changed a lot, I mean, I don’t know how to explain it. When you’re at work, you think about your daughter, you want to come home earlier, you want to hold her, you want her – I mean, you have more beautiful moments – but it’s hard to explain. I don’t know how to explain it.”.

You were also used as a full-back, but now you only play as a centre-back….

Sources indicate that “Good, good, because I also consider myself a centre-back, but it’s true that I can also play full-back. It’s something I can do, but it’s not my favourite position. But yes, it’s true that I’ve played a few games there in the past, but I’m happy playing as a centre back and I’m happy that the coach sees that too.”.

“I mean, crazy in a good way, yes. He likes to have fun, he likes to dance, he likes to talk, so he’s a bright spot, as they say, for the locker room, yes.”.

“Well, that’s a good question. Yes, I miss her. I thought about it even when the little girl was born: I also want to score a goal, I mean, dedicate a goal to her, so I miss her, yes.”.

How do you concentrate when you’re in the hotel retreat? How do you focus in the hours leading up to kick-off?

According to recent reports, “It’s become a routine now, so I always do the same things. You’re in the hotel, you take a shower, you play a little video game or you’re on your phone, so now I don’t even think about it, it’s really become a routine.”.

What does Maignan ask of you, defenders?

“He says to stay focused on the game because, as we know, one moment can change the game and at Milan it can also change a season, so it’s very important not to underestimate every moment and always stay focused.

It seems to me that there is a great understanding between you and Strahinja Pavlovic even off the pitch….

It has been revealed that “Yes, it’s true, he and I have a good relationship; we met last year. Then when you see him you might not think, I mean, I didn’t think he would be such a great friend, but we got along really well both on and off the pitch, it’s really nice to spend time with him.”.

Industry observers note that our 007s at Milanello tell us about some great ping pong matches between you and Pavlovic. Who’s the better player?

“This is difficult, but he started at a much higher level than me. But now I’ve improved a lot, although I have to say he’s even stronger. But yes, every day we start with a game of ping pong and then we start working.”.

According to recent reports, would you like your daughter to play soccer in the future? Are you planning a second child? Would you like to have a son who plays soccer?

Sources indicate that “I want her to do what she wants, where she feels good, where she doesn’t feel pressured, and where she can express herself best. And then, going back to ping pong, I think there’s some video; maybe we can see me beat her.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stoke City have leapfrogged Birmingham City in the Championship table after a narrow 1-0 victory over the Blues at the bet365 Stadium on Saturday, as Potters wing-back Luca Bombino sends a message to the home supporters.

Stoke have climbed to 2nd in the Championship table after beating Birmingham at the weekend, remaining level on points with Middlesbrough, but with a slightly worse goal difference than the Teesside outfit.

The Potters, following their victory over Blues, have become the first club in the division to win ten league games this season, as one player has sent a message to supporters after his day ended early.

George Hirst's goal just after half-time would prove to be the decisive one, as the Scottish forward netted just his second goal for Stoke following his potential £10 million move from Ipswich Town over the summer.

With the home side in control and looking for a second, American wing-back Luca Bombino mistimed his challenge on Patrick Roberts whilst already on a yellow card, as referee Robert Madley had no choice but to give the 20-year-old his marching orders just past the hour mark.

Stoke withstood everything Birmingham could throw at them, and Bombino's red card ultimately didn't affect the result, as the American has taken to social media to share a message with supporters.

In his post, the 20-year-old apologised for his mistake, made known how proud he is of his teammates' performance despite his blunder, and thanked the Stoke fans for their support.

His red card means he will miss his side's Championship home clash with Millwall on Wednesday evening, where either Eric Bocat or Justin Devenny will presumably take his role at left wing-back, as Stoke supporters have shared their thoughts over Bombino's red.

After three defeats to open the campaign, Stoke have responded with an incredible ten wins in their next 13 league games and are flying.

Bombino's red card was the only damp spot on a bright day for the Potters on Saturday, as Stoke fans have taken to social media to react to the American's sending-off.

Stoke fans are no different to many other sets of supporters, in that they love a tackle, and they adore 110 per cent effort, as Bombino epitomises that.

The only thing the American can do now is learn from this situation and ensure similar mistakes don't happen moving forward.

Stoke supporters will always forgive a player as long as they give it their all and show passion, and in Bombino's case, he has likely already been forgiven by the masses.

This Potters fan backs the 20-year-old to get just fine at the club.

Either Bocat or Devenny will take Bombino's place at left wing-back against Millwall midweek, as Bombino will have to fight his way back into the side upon his return.

Bombino had only played for San Diego in the MLS before his move to North Staffordshire in the summer, and whilst his rawness prevailed in this game, there is belief he will come good in due course.

What do you make of Bombino's red card? Can Stoke continue to sustain this level of form moving forward? How do you see the Potters faring from here on out? Share your thoughts below.

With his side claiming a huge three points against promotion rivals Birmingham, Stoke manager Mark Robins will have no intention of slowing down anytime soon.

Millwall and West Ham United await the Potters next week, as whilst both will pose different threats, the former Coventry City boss will be heading into each clash with an abundance of confidence.

It's been a decade since Stoke last recorded a top-half finish in any division they have been in, and Robins will look to destroy that record and then some, with a spot back in the Premier League in his sights.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

QPR have had a brilliant start to the season, and the prospect of finishing in a play-off spot for the first time since their relegation to the Championship way back in 2015 seems a lot more attainable as the year goes on.

Julien Stephan's side currently occupy the final position in the revamped play-offs and are playing some of the best football in the second tier, per the underlying numbers. They have the fourth-best xG difference in the league, and only Middlesbrough and Wolves have a better xGA.

A lot of the players who QPR signed in the past few seasons, either from League One or as youngsters from Premier League clubs and abroad, are starting to blossom into very good top-end Championship players, and it's being reflected in their results.

According to recent reports, there's apt depth everywhere in the squad, perhaps other than in central midfield. Ball-playing centre-back Ronnie Edwards, who has played in the engine room before at Peterborough United, has been called in to deputise at times, either due to Nicolas Madsen's injury or a lack of form for Jonathan Varane.

Glen Kamara was QPR's marquee midfield signing this past summer, with the former play-off finalist at Leeds United joining on loan to form an engine room core with Madsen and Varane.

However, the Hoops' unlucky history with injuries in recent times caught up with Madsen, who should be back shortly. But it did leave Julien Stephan light in those areas and, as mentioned, Edwards was called in to deputise as Kamara worked his way into the side, coming in instead of Varane.

Therefore, FLW's QPR fan pundit, Louis Moir, wants to see his side bolster their midfield options in case injury strikes again, and would like to see Fulham's Harrison Reed arrive on loan.

Industry observers note that "One player I'd like to see join, and I'm not sure it's even that ambitious, is Harrison Reed. I've always liked him as a player across the years; he's really tidy, neat, does the hard work and has shown his ability in the Premier League," he said.

"I think with this season, Madsen has been out a bit, Kamara has obviously come in and has been class, but Varane hasn't been at his best, so we're kind of lacking in midfield.

It has been revealed that "You never want a serious injury to occur to someone like Kamara, for example, and Edwards has come in and done a great job in midfield, but I just feel we could do with one more, and that's mainly due to Varane not being at his best. I think it [the midfield] can be a weak point if Madsen or Kamara are out.".

Varane was one of QPR's best performers pre-Stephan, to the point where the Hoops were reportedly rejecting £4 million offers from La Liga side Espanyol for his services. There is a player there, but that hasn't been seen this season, especially. With Reed in the squad, the R's could maintain this early-season play-off form if injuries do continue to haunt them.

Sources indicate that reed is well-respected at Fulham and has been a great servant to the club in the seven years he's been playing at Craven Cottage. However, the club is starting to outgrow the 31-year-old.

Industry observers note that he made just seven league appearances last season, remaining unused from the bench on 22 separate occasions. Funnily enough, one of those cameo bench appearances saw him score the Premier League's Goal of the Season in a 2-2 draw with Liverpool in January.

This season, under Alvaro Arbeloa, Reed's role in the squad has decreased even further. Now, the midfielder isn't getting into matchday squads in the Premier League, and all his appearances so far have been in the EFL Cup.

Do you think Harrison Reed will be a primary loan target for Championship sides this summer? Let us know in the comments.

"I think Reed may be of interest to a few Championship clubs," says Moir, due to his standing in the Fulham fold. "But him on loan would be more than ideal and a really top signing.

Industry observers note that "I think it's more than realistic, more than ambitious, and would fit in really well. He'd add a lot of bite to the midfield and more depth. You wouldn't have to worry about him starting each week, but he'd come on and do a good job.".

It has been revealed that reed's long-term future at Fulham is up in the air. The 31-year-old's four-year deal, which he signed back in 2023, is up at the end of the campaign.

There is an option for the Cottagers to extend that by a year, but the likelihood of that happening seems quite slim, especially if Arbeloa's side remain in the Premier League this season.

So, Reed could be in a situation where a loan move in January could almost be a way for a loaning team to have a six-month trial before a decision is made about handing him a longer-term contract.

Sources indicate that if QPR remain a Championship side, this could definitely be a decision that they make. Reed has 131 Premier League appearances and has won promotion from the Championship twice with Fulham. At 32, he could be the perfect veteran option in the middle for a side that were on the cusp of promotion and want to go again in 2027/28.

Obviously, the Hoops will want to go up this year, and Reed could help aid in that, too, but thinking longer term, getting the 31-year-old through the door could be quite an underrated move for this R's side.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 07:00 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 08:12 EST, 19 November 2026.

Secure the king, and the rest will follow.

Much of the attention surrounding Arsenal in recent months was on Mikel Arteta’s contract, which had been due to expire next summer. Behind the scenes, sporting director Andrea Berta lined up the Spaniard’s fresh four-year deal, which he signed in October, all the while keeping one eye on the players central to the club's long-term vision.

News of latest contracts for Declan Rice, Jurrien Timber, David Raya and Piero Hincapie all broke in the past 72 hours. Extending players when they're approaching the final two years of their contract isn't revolutionary, but the spate of them in such quick succession drew the eye.

Most of the deals have been months in the making – talks over Rice’s new contract stretch back to at least March, for example. It also comes after Real Madrid having monitored Rice and Raya for the past year, and Barcelona trying to lure Hincapie away back in June.

This push is central to Arsenal’s desire to forge a dynasty by securing the nucleus of this team for at least the next four years of Arteta's reign, following Gabriel, William Saliba and Bukayo Saka all signing long-term contracts last year.

Arsenal are closing in on new contracts for (L-R) David Raya, Declan Rice and Jurrien Timber, after also tying down Gabriel and William Saliba last year.

Piero Hincapie (left) is also set to agree new terms, with the rush of extensions coming after manager Mikel Arteta (right) signed a four-year deal last month.

An agent who has previously dealt with Arsenal revealed why the strategy is beneficial to multiple parties.

He told Daily Mail Sport: ‘They are maintaining the value of their players and ensuring squad continuity, to avoid the possibility of disruption. Now Mikel has got the right blend of players and got rid of the agitators (from earlier in his reign), he wants to keep the group solid.

‘Too many clubs leave it too late when it comes to contract extensions and sometimes agents are happy to let a contract run down so they can renew from a position of strength. Signing-on fees for both the agent and player, higher wages and commission can be boosted.

‘Though on the flipside, an agent can renegotiate a contract with two more years remaining and say: “If you want us to extend now, we want signing bonuses et cetera”. It also provides further long-term security for your client. It’s smart business all round. Arsenal are champions, the players are happy, why wouldn’t you extend?’.

Rice benefits the most – his pay rise will take him very close to Saka, Arsenal’s top earner, with the winger on a deal worth £350,000 a week.

Now, though, comes the tricky part: who of the remaining first-team squad do they want to commit to? Extending every senior player’s contract in a Premier League world governed by Squad Cost Ratio rules is not particularly feasible. The proposal to make up to 60 job cuts across the club, for instance, is a reminder of the general financial stakes at play.

In a recent development, the biggest decisions are on the futures of Martin Odegaard and Kai Havertz, both of whom have contracts expiring in 2028. One is the club’s captain, and the other is Arteta’s favourite son.

Recent findings suggest that the injuries and dip in form of the two men last season could be why Arsenal may bide their time. Odegaard managed just 16 league starts with shoulder, knee and muscular problems disrupting his campaign, having also missed a large chunk of the season before with an ankle problem.

Kai Havertz (second left) and club captain Martin Odegaard (second right) are the next big decisions for Arteta. Both are key men but is the time right to capitalise on their sale value?

According to recent reports, havertz's season was even more frustrating, suffering a knee injury on the opening day which required surgery, before subsequent muscular setbacks. He played 90 minutes just once in the title-winning campaign.

Both remain important to Arteta, but their previous injuries and potentially strong sale value makes committing to improved long-term contracts a more difficult financial decision.

Sources indicate that mikel Merino’s deal expires in 2028, but he is not in the same financial or importance bracket as the above two stars. Ben White’s contract is also up in 2028, but there is an option to trigger a 12-month extension. This group are all in or approaching their peak years: Odegaard and Havertz are 27, White is 29 and Merino is 30.

Sources indicate that given most of the players who have agreed new long-term contracts will be past 30 by the time their deals expire, there has to be an awareness of not letting this squad get too old. The average age of Arsenal's starting XI in the Premier League this season is exactly 27 years old. Manchester United (27 years and 86 days) are the only Substantial Six side whose XIs have been older, while perennial rivals Manchester City are 480 days younger per player.

More broadly, sources say the rush of senior players committing their future to the champions is as much about the healthy culture at the club as it is about the team’s strong chance of scooping up silverware in the seasons ahead.

It has been revealed that the environment is a positive one (winning a league title helps, of course) and the players are close with one another. They enjoy going into work, which can’t be stated for stars at every club in the league.

Sources indicate that there’s a recognition among players of Arteta’s ability to improve them, both individually and tactically. The Spaniard is a stickler for detail and doesn’t believe in the notion of a ‘finished product’.

In a recent development, when Rice arrived in July 2023 on the pre-season tour of the US as Arsenal's £105million club-record signing, Arteta described his newly introduced midfielder as a ‘lighthouse’. Yet last month after the club’s 2-1 victory over Leeds, the manager noted: ‘I went to him (Rice) and said, “You are not the lighthouse anymore. You are something else”.’.

Even Rice is not safe from Arteta's relentless demands for improvement.

The collective trust built between Arteta and his players has created a setting where constant improvement is an expectation. And the players want to do that at Arsenal.

This season, Rice has been challenged to impact play more in the final third. The collective trust built between Arteta and his squad has created a setting where constant improvement is an expectation, rather than a desire. And the players want to achieve that at Arsenal, rather than anywhere else.

Berta deserves a pat on the back, too. Ex-sporting director Edu, a shrewd people person and operator, did a fine job with the cards he was dealt; Saliba, Gabriel and Rice arrived on his watch. Berta has had a very different deck of cards to play with, but has also done well to turn this group into champions.

Much of Arsenal’s nucleus is now secured. But there are tricky decisions still to come for Arteta and Berta.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Derby County have been one of the surprise packages in the Championship so far this season, but for all the wrong reasons.

The Rams sit 23rd in the table after 16 games with just 10 points to their name, and their misery was compounded after returning from the international break with a 2-0 defeat at the hands of Southampton on Saturday.

Recent findings suggest that there was a sense of optimism around Pride Park ahead of the start of the new season. After last term's excellent eighth place finish and the expansion of the play-offs, there was a real sense that Derby could finally have a crack at promotion to the Premier League.

John Eustace had worked wonders since his arrival in February 2025, building a squad that was seemingly capable of fighting at the sharp end of the Championship.

However, with just one win in 14 league matches to start the upcoming season, the Rams were left cut adrift with Burnley and Preston in the relegation zone, with no escape looking likely.

A much-needed victory over Bolton Wanderers in the final game before the early November international break gave supporters hope that things could turn around, but Saturday's defeat at St Mary's was a depressing thud back down to reality.

Following Saturday's defeat at Southampton, Rams defender Dion Sanderson faced BBC Sport Derby to give his verdict on a difficult run of fixtures ahead, and it's fair to say his words will cut deep for supporters.

"Everything's different, different teams, we prepare differently each week," Sanderson said.

"But I think from a personal note, it doesn't matter what team you're up against, you've got to play for the badge on your shirt, play for the club, and play for yourself, a bit of pride.

Sources indicate that "I think the lads this week, especially, have got to continue [the intensity in training]. We've got to take that onto next week and the week after.

Recent findings suggest that "We are in a relegation scrap and that's the reality of it. The lads need to start pulling their socks up now, and we're asking a lot from everyone," the defender concluded.

After just 16 games, a player admitting that a relegation scrap is on the cards certainly isn't what fans will want to be hearing, especially after how much optimism there was heading into the season.

After the interview with Sanderson was posted to X by BBC Sport Derby, some Rams supporters reacted to what their centre-back had to say in the wake of yet another disappointing defeat.

One fan remained surprisingly positive, suggesting Derby did enough to earn a point and encouraged the players to keep their heads up.

Another wasn't quite as forgiving, calling Sanderson 'hopeless'.

Another also voiced their frustrations at Sanderson himself, suggesting he should let his performances do the talking rather than post-match interviews.

Finally, one fan blamed club CEO Stephen Pearce for the mess the club right now finds itself in, and suggested nothing will get better until he is replaced.

Injury-induced signalling coordinates immunity and cannibalism in locusts

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 91 min read (18150 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~91 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cannibalism, the consumption of conspecifics, is widespread across the animal kingdom and can profoundly influence individual fitness and population dynamics1,2.
  • Cannibalism, the consumption of conspecifics, is widespread across the animal kingdom and is often considered to be an adaptive behaviour driven by ecological or social pressures1,2.
  • In a recent development, locusts provide a compelling model for studies of cannibalism because of its vital role in collective dynamics5,6.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cannibalism, the consumption of conspecifics, is widespread across the animal kingdom and can profoundly influence individual fitness and population dynamics1,2. Although the ecological and social conditions that favour cannibalism have been well documented2, the molecular signals that trigger cannibalistic attacks have remained poorly understood. Here we show that in Locusta migratoria, guaiacol, a volatile compound with augmented release after injury, attracts gregarious nymphs and induces cannibalistic behaviour. Guaiacol is detected by olfactory receptors LmOR36 and LmOR34, and disruption of either receptor abolishes attraction, thereby impairing induction of cannibalism. Guaiacol is synthesized by haemolymph symbiont Enterobacter hormaechei. Injury promotes bacterial congregation at the wound site, leading to elevated guaiacol production through a clustered set of vanillic acid decarboxylase genes; deletion of this gene cluster abolishes guaiacol production and its behavioural effects. Notably, guaiacol initially functions as a beneficial signal after injury. Guaiacol activates immune-related pathways in wounded locusts, enhancing pathogen resistance and increasing survival following minor injury. However, when guaiacol emission exceeds a threshold determined by injury severity, it functions as an external cue that attracts cannibals. Cannibalistic locusts exploit this immune-related odour to locate severely injured conspecifics, gaining both nutritional resources and immune system benefits. Together, our findings identify a microbial–chemical mechanism that links immune defence with cannibalistic behaviour and provide potential molecular targets for manipulation of cannibalism-dependent population dynamics.

Cannibalism, the consumption of conspecifics, is widespread across the animal kingdom and is often considered to be an adaptive behaviour driven by ecological or social pressures1,2. However, its occurrence is highly context-dependent, and the underlying regulatory mechanisms remain poorly understood. In humans, cannibalism largely disappeared with cultural evolution, partly owing to prion diseases3. Similarly, insects such as crickets rarely engage in cannibalism under normal conditions, but confinement or nutritional deprivation can trigger this behaviour4. These observations highlight the influence of environmental pressures on cannibalism, although its intrinsic regulatory mechanisms remain unclear.

In a recent development, locusts provide a compelling model for studies of cannibalism because of its vital role in collective dynamics5,6. In juvenile migratory bands, the threat of conspecific predation from behind promotes forward movement, reducing cannibalistic risk and contributing to group cohesion5,6. Cannibalism also provides nutritional benefits, allowing locusts to compensate for food deficiencies and potentially enhancing survival and movement capacity7,8. This behaviour is strongly influenced by density-dependent phase polyphenism. At low densities, solitarious locusts avoid conspecifics, whereas increased population density promotes gregarious behaviour and cannibalistic encounters5,7. Nutritional deficiencies further exacerbate cannibalism. Field studies of South American locusts (Schistocerca cancellata) have demonstrated that carbohydrate deprivation promotes cannibalism9, whereas laboratory studies on desert locusts (Schistocerca gregaria) have shown that protein-biased diets reduce movement and increase cannibalistic interactions7. Although these findings establish the ecological importance of cannibalism, its molecular and genetic regulation remains poorly understood.

Chemical cues regulate diverse locust behaviours, including aggregation10,11, oviposition12, mating13 and cannibalism14. Our previous work identified phenylacetonitrile (PAN) as a density-dependent anticannibalistic pheromone that activates specific olfactory receptors and reduces conspecific predation in crowded populations14. However, whether chemical cues actively induce cannibalism has remained unclear. Field and laboratory observations indicate that injured locusts are preferentially targeted by conspecifics15, suggesting that injury-induced chemical signals may attract individuals and promote cannibalistic behaviour.

According to recent reports, guaiacol, a volatile compound produced by gut microbiota during plant digestion, has been identified as an aggregation pheromone in desert locusts16. Here we show that injury-induced microbiota-derived guaiacol coordinates immune defence and cannibalism in migratory locusts (Locusta migratoria) and elucidate the underlying mechanisms, which span microbial biosynthesis, olfactory detection, immune regulation and behavioural responses. Together, our findings identify a microbial signalling mechanism linking immunity and cannibalism, revealing how host–microbe interactions mediate a trade-off between immune protection and vulnerability to conspecific predation.

It has been revealed that cannibalism in L. migratoria exhibits phase polyphenism, with solitarious nymphs typically avoiding conspecific predation, whereas gregarious nymphs are more prone to engage in cannibalism, particularly under conditions of crowding or food scarcity14. Preliminary observations indicated that injured individuals were rapidly surrounded and attacked by nearby conspecifics (Fig. 1a), suggesting that injury itself serves as a cue that increases susceptibility to conspecific predation. To test this hypothesis, we conducted dual-choice assays with gregarious fourth- and fifth-instar nymphs, the developmental stages at which cannibalism is most prevalent14. As injury can alter locomotor performance and therefore influence predator choice independently of injury-derived signals, we controlled for this potentially confounding factor by immobilizing both prey individuals. This experimental design enabled us to specifically evaluate the contribution of injury-associated cues to predator preference. In each assay, pairs of immobilized intact and injured fourth-instar nymphs were presented at opposite ends of a chamber containing ten starved fifth-instar predators (Fig. 1b). Injuries were induced either mechanically or by previous conspecific bites. Across all assays, predators consistently exhibited a marked predation preference for injured over intact prey, indicating a significant role of injury in heightening vulnerability to conspecific predation (Fig. 1c).

It has been revealed that to determine whether the type of injury influenced predation preference, we compared predator preferences between mechanically injured and bitten prey. No significant difference was observed (Fig. 1c), indicating that injury alone, regardless of its origin, is sufficient to induce preferential predation. To explore whether injury-induced vulnerability was consistent across developmental stages, we extended the assays to first- to fifth-instar nymphs as prey. In all stages tested, fifth-instar predators consistently preferred injured prey over their intact counterparts, irrespective of injury type (Extended Data Fig. 1a). These findings demonstrate that injury-driven cannibalism is a robust and consistent trait across the development of gregarious locusts.

Next, we investigated the sensory cues mediating injury-induced predation. To assess the roles of olfactory and visual inputs, we performed antennal ablation (disrupting primary olfactory input), knocked out olfactory coreceptor LmOrco (disrupting olfactory receptor function) (Extended Data Fig. 1b) or removed the compound eyes (disrupting visual input). Predators with removed compound eyes retained their preference for injured prey (Fig. 1d), suggesting that visual cues are not required to mediate this behaviour. By contrast, predators lacking antennae or LmOrco function showed no preference for injured over intact prey (Fig. 1e,f). Notably, although antennectomized predators no longer exhibited a statistically significant preference, a weak residual bias towards injured prey remained (Fig. 1e). This observation was consistent with the anatomical organization of the locust olfactory system, in which the antennae constitute the principal but not the exclusive olfactory organs. Consequently, antennal removal might substantially reduce but not completely eliminate olfactory perception. By contrast, disruption of LmOrco, which broadly impairs odorant receptor function, resulted in a complete loss of discriminatory behaviour (Fig. 1f). Together, these findings identify LmOrco-dependent olfaction as the primary sensory modality mediating injury-induced cannibalistic predation.

According to recent reports, finally, we assessed whether volatile chemical cues contributed to the observed predation bias. Headspace volatiles from both injured and intact nymphs were collected and presented in a dual-choice olfactometer (Fig. 1g). Starved fifth-instar predators strongly preferred the zone containing volatiles from injured individuals over the zone containing volatiles from intact prey (Fig. 1h). No significant difference in preference was observed between volatiles from mechanically versus bitten prey (Fig. 1h), indicating that injury-induced volatile release enhances predator attraction, thereby increasing the susceptibility of injured individuals to cannibalism. By contrast, LmOrco−/− predators showed no preference for the zone containing volatiles from injured individuals (Fig. 1i), indicating that LmOrco-dependent olfaction mediated the predation preference.

According to recent reports, to investigate the chemical signals underlying injury-induced cannibalism in L. migratoria, we analysed the headspace volatiles emitted by intact, mechanically injured and bitten locust nymphs (Fig. 2a). Among the compounds detected, guaiacol emerged as the dominant injury-affected odorant (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Table 1), with emission levels approximately ten-fold higher in injured nymphs compared with intact controls and gregarious adults (Fig. 2b,c and Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). This increase in guaiacol release was consistent across all developmental instars (first to fifth) (Extended Data Fig. 2c), suggesting that an increase in guaiacol production is a consistent physiological response to injury in gregarious nymphs. By contrast, other compounds—including PAN, which has previously been linked to suppression of cannibalism14—showed no significant changes across injury conditions (Fig. 2b,c and Extended Data Fig. 2d), indicating that guaiacol is a key injury cue.

In a recent development, to assess the behavioural significance of guaiacol, we conducted dual-choice olfactometer assays with fifth-instar nymphs and male and female adults from both gregarious and solitarious phases, testing the effects of synthetic guaiacol (Extended Data Table 2) at a concentration of 10−3 (Fig. 2d). Only gregarious nymphs exhibited strong attraction to guaiacol; solitarious individuals and gregarious adults highlighted no significant preference (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Video 1). This indicated that guaiacol selectively attracts gregarious nymphs. We then investigated whether the naturally emitted levels of guaiacol from injured gregarious nymphs were sufficient to trigger attraction. Quantitative headspace analysis showed that emissions from injured gregarious nymphs corresponded to concentrations equivalent to 10−5 to 10−4 dilutions of synthetic guaiacol (Extended Data Fig. 2e). To determine whether these natural guaiacol emissions were sufficient to induce attraction, we tested behavioural responses of gregarious nymphs using a full concentration series (10−7 to 10−2) in a two-choice olfactometer (Fig. 2d). Attraction to guaiacol emerged sharply at 10−6 and remained robust at higher concentrations but disappeared at 10−7 (Fig. 2f). This aligned with the physiological range of natural emissions from injured nymphs, confirming that guaiacol concentrations released by injured individuals are behaviourally relevant. As all preceding behavioural assays were conducted with individually tested locusts, we next examined whether guaiacol attraction was preserved under the social conditions that characterize gregarious populations. To address this question, we performed dual-choice olfactometer assays using groups of five gregarious nymphs and quantified the average time spent by the group on each side of the arena. Consistent with the results obtained from individually tested animals, groups of gregarious nymphs spent significantly more time on the side containing 10−3 guaiacol than on the control side (Extended Data Fig. 2f and Supplementary Video 2). These findings demonstrate that the attractive effect of guaiacol persists in a group context and therefore probably operates under ecologically relevant social conditions.

It has been revealed that as attraction alone does not necessarily imply a decision to engage in cannibalistic behaviour, we next investigated whether guaiacol could directly trigger cannibalistic predation. We performed two-choice predation assays, providing pairs of intact fourth-instar gregarious nymphs—one treated with 2 µl of 10−4 guaiacol (representing natural emission levels from injured nymphs) (Extended Data Fig. 2e) and the other with solvent oil—to 10 starved fifth-instar gregarious predators (Fig. 2g). Guaiacol-treated nymphs were preferentially consumed, whereas solvent-treated nymphs were rarely attacked (Fig. 2h), confirming that guaiacol is a potent elicitor of cannibalistic predation. We then sought to rule out the potential influence of endogenous guaiacol on predator preference. Previous studies have shown that guaiacol is primarily synthesized by gut microbiota during plant digestion in locusts16. To eliminate this confounding factor, we generated germ-depleted gregarious nymphs by administering a cocktail of three antibiotics (tetracycline, streptomycin and ciprofloxacin) in their feed17,18,19 (Fig. 2i). This approach effectively abolished guaiacol emission in both intact and injured nymphs, providing a chemically clean background for subsequent behavioural assays (Fig. 2j). We then treated the germ-depleted gregarious nymphs with 2 µl of either 10−4 guaiacol (mimicking natural release from injured nymphs) (Extended Data Fig. 2e) or solvent oil and used them as prey in dual-choice predation assays (Fig. 2i). As observed previously, guaiacol-treated nymphs were preferentially attacked, and solvent-treated nymphs were largely ignored (Fig. 2k and Extended Data Fig. 2g). Finally, to evaluate the ecological relevance of guaiacol-mediated cannibalism under more naturalistic conditions, we performed semi-field experiments in large outdoor mesh enclosures (1.8 m × 1.2 m × 1.5 m). Each enclosure contained 500 fifth-instar gregarious predators, together with 100 fourth-instar prey perfumed with either 10−4 guaiacol or solvent alone (Extended Data Fig. 2h). After 24 h, substantially fewer fourth-instar nymphs remained in guaiacol-treated enclosures than in control enclosures, indicating a significantly higher frequency of cannibalistic interactions in the presence of guaiacol (Extended Data Fig. 2h). Consistent with direct behavioural observations, the reduction in surviving individuals was attributable to increased conspecific predation rather than escape, as all locusts were confined within the enclosure. These findings demonstrate that guaiacol-mediated promotion of cannibalism persists at the population level under seminatural conditions, supporting the ecological relevance of this injury-associated signal. Collectively, these findings establish guaiacol as a critical chemical cue that both signals injury and induces conspecific predation.

Recent findings suggest that to elucidate the molecular basis of guaiacol detection in L. migratoria, we sought to identify the specific olfactory receptors involved. In our previous study, we identified LmOR34, LmOR36 and LmOR39 as receptors responsive to guaiacol, on the basis of functional characterization of 49 L. migratoria olfactory receptors20. To confirm whether other olfactory receptors were involved in detection of this compound, we expanded our analysis to include a panel of 82 of approximately 140 identified L. migratoria olfactory receptors (Fig. 3a). Consistent with our earlier findings, LmOR34, LmOR36 and LmOR39 exhibited robust responses to guaiacol in a heterologous expression system (Fig. 3a,b), while no other receptor revealed comparable sensitivity.

According to recent reports, olfactory sensory neurons expressing different olfactory receptors are localized in distinct sensilla on the antennae of L. migratoria. To identify the sensilla responsible for guaiacol detection, we performed single-sensillum recordings (SSR) from basiconic and trichoid sensilla, which contain neurons expressing coreceptor Orco21,22. Basiconic sensilla harbour a larger population of sensory neurons (20–50), whereas trichoid sensilla contain only 2 or 3 neurons14. Owing to the higher neuronal density in basiconic sensilla, individual responses could not be distinguished on the basis of action potential amplitudes. Therefore, we measured the aggregate response of the entire neuronal population within the sensillum. Strong neuronal responses to guaiacol were detected in basiconic sensilla, whereas no response was observed in trichoid sensilla (Fig. 3c).

Inconsistent results were noted between electrophysiological and behavioural tests with respect to active concentrations of guaiacol, with a significantly higher threshold in the electrophysiological experiments. However, when we used solid-phase microextraction (SPME) technology to measure the concentration that actually reached the antenna during stimulation in the electrophysiological experiments, we found that the amount of guaiacol was comparable with the 10−6 dilution used in the behavioural assays (Extended Data Fig. 3a).

Sources indicate that to assess the functional contribution of the LmOR34, LmOR36 and LmOR39 genes in vivo, we generated targeted loss-of-function mutants using CRISPR–Cas9-mediated genome editing. Guide RNAs (Extended Data Table 3) targeting the first exon of these genes produced frame-shift deletions of 235 bp (LmOR34) (Extended Data Fig. 3b), 262 bp (LmOR36) (Extended Data Fig. 3b) and 8 bp (LmOR39) (Extended Data Fig. 3b), resulting in predicted truncations of the encoded proteins. Electroantennography (EAG) recordings revealed that the guaiacol-induced response was significantly reduced in LmOR34−/− and LmOR36−/− mutants compared with wild-type nymphs, whereas the response in LmOR39−/− mutants remained unchanged (Fig. 3d). Furthermore, SSR recordings from basiconic sensilla demonstrated that neuronal response to guaiacol was significantly reduced in the LmOR34−/− and LmOR36−/− mutants compared with wild-type nymphs, whereas LmOR39−/− locusts exhibited robust responses (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 3c). Taken together, these data indicate key roles of both LmOR34 and LmOR36 in mediation of the detection of guaiacol. We then investigated the behavioural consequences of these receptor disruptions. LmOR34−/− and LmOR36−/− mutants showed a complete lack of attraction to guaiacol (Fig. 3f), in contrast to wild-type controls, which exhibited robust attraction. This loss of attraction was accompanied by a marked impairment in predation preference for guaiacol-treated prey nymphs (Fig. 3g). By contrast, the LmOR39−/− mutants showed no alteration in their behavioural and predation preferences (Fig. 3f,g), suggesting that LmOR34 and LmOR36 are essential for mediation of the behavioural response to guaiacol.

Our previous study revealed that LmOR34 and LmOR36 also responded strongly to 2,4,6-trimethylpyridine (2,4,6-TMP)20 (Extended Data Fig. 3d), a compound that is highly attractive to gregarious locusts. To test whether this compound also promoted cannibalistic behaviour, we performed dual-choice predation assays (Extended Data Fig. 3e), presenting prey nymphs treated with either 2,4,6-TMP or solvent to starved gregarious predators. Predator nymphs showed no significant preference for 2,4,6-TMP-treated prey compared with controls (Extended Data Fig. 3e). These results showed that although 2,4,6-TMP is a potent attractant, it does not directly promote cannibalism, confirming that this compound has other ecological functions. To directly compare the effects of guaiacol and 2,4,6-TMP on cannibalistic behaviour, we conducted a second dual-choice assay, in which prey nymphs were treated with either guaiacol or 2,4,6-TMP, both at a 10−4 dilution. Predator nymphs showed a strong preference for guaiacol-treated prey over 2,4,6-TMP-treated prey (Extended Data Fig. 3e). To further examine whether the observed predatory preference reflected a general response to behaviourally attractive locust volatiles, we performed a further dual-choice predation assay using 4-vinylanisole (4VA), another attractive locust odorant10. Predators were simultaneously offered two germ-depleted gregarious nymphs, one treated with 2 μl of a 10−4 dilution of guaiacol and the other with an equal volume of a 10−4 dilution of 4VA. Predator nymphs showed a significantly stronger preference for attacking and biting guaiacol-treated prey than 4VA-treated prey (Extended Data Fig. 3e). Together, these results demonstrate that enhanced predatory responses are not elicited by attractive locust volatiles in general but are specific to guaiacol, identifying guaiacol as a specialized chemical cue that promotes cannibalistic behaviour.

Notably, ligand-specific behavioural divergence despite shared receptor components has been widely documented across insects, including model species Drosophila melanogaster23,24, in which differential peripheral tuning25 and downstream circuit integration enable discrimination of chemically related cues26. To examine whether similar mechanisms operated in locusts, we compared the response properties of LmOR34 and LmOR36 to guaiacol and 2,4,6-TMP. Although both ligands activated both receptors, guaiacol elicited markedly stronger and more sensitive responses than 2,4,6-TMP (Extended Data Fig. 3f,g). Moreover, the response kinetics of LmOR34 and LmOR36 differed substantially between guaiacol and 2,4,6-TMP (Extended Data Fig. 3h,i), indicating that these ligands impose distinct temporal activation patterns at the receptor level that could be differentially decoded by downstream circuits. In addition to receptor-intrinsic differences, ligand-specific behaviours are likely to be shaped by distinct population-level coding in the antennal lobe. Consistent with this idea, our previous study showed that the antennal lobe activation patterns evoked by guaiacol and 2,4,6-TMP only partially overlapped27, suggesting other receptor inputs. For example, LmOR46 responds to 2,4,6-TMP (Extended Data Fig. 3d), whereas LmOR39 responds to guaiacol (Fig. 3b). Furthermore, because only 82 of the 140 predicted L. migratoria olfactory receptors have been functionally characterized, other receptors may remain unidentified. Although these receptors may contribute only modestly to odour detection, even weak inputs could reshape ensemble coding in the antennal lobe, thereby biasing downstream circuit activation towards distinct ecological and behavioural outcomes. Together, differential receptor tuning (sensitivity and kinetics) and ligand-specific recruitment of other receptors probably explain why guaiacol and 2,4,6-TMP produce divergent behavioural consequences despite engaging shared receptors.

Recent findings suggest that guaiacol has previously been identified as a volatile produced by Pantoea agglomerans in the gut of S. gregaria and has been implicated in locust behaviour16. To identify guaiacol-producing bacteria in L. migratoria, we performed gut microbiota metagenomic sequencing but did not detect P. agglomerans (Fig. 4a), suggesting alternative microbial sources. We subsequently isolated cultivable bacteria from the gut and haemolymph of fourth-instar gregarious nymphs (Fig. 4b). Screening of more than 50 colonies identified a guaiacol-producing isolate from both tissues (Fig. 4b,c), which whole-genome sequencing identified as Enterobacter hormaechei, a dominant gut bacterium (Fig. 4a). Metagenomic analyses further confirmed high abundance of this bacterium in both the gut and haemolymph (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 4a). Although E. hormaechei was not reported in a previous study of the L. migratoria microbiome28, metagenomic sequencing and quantitative PCR (qPCR) detected it in all six geographically distinct field populations examined, with varying relative abundances (Extended Data Fig. 4b). Screening of other isolates also identified Klebsiella pneumoniae as a guaiacol producer, with emission levels comparable with those of E. hormaechei (Fig. 4c). However, we selected E. hormaechei for subsequent mechanistic analyses as it was consistently detected across samples and populations and exhibited stable guaiacol production.

Sources indicate that we next examined the relationships of injury with bacterial abundance and guaiacol emission. Following injury, both haemolymph bacterial loads (Fig. 4d) and guaiacol emission (Fig. 4e) increased over time, peaking approximately 6 h after injury and stabilizing at around 8 h (Fig. 4d,e), and their temporal changes were positively correlated (Fig. 4f). To assess localized bacterial enrichment, we collected equal volumes of haemolymph from wound sites and intact regions of the same individuals 6 h after injury (Fig. 4g). Wound-site haemolymph had significantly higher bacterial loads (Fig. 4h) and guaiacol levels (Fig. 4i), indicating localized accumulation of E. hormaechei and enhanced guaiacol production. As population density can influence locust gut microbiota29, we also compared E. hormaechei abundance between phases and found no significant difference between solitarious and gregarious nymphs (Extended Data Fig. 4c).

Sources indicate that to determine whether E. hormaechei influenced locust behaviour, we first tested its volatiles in a two-choice olfactometer (Fig. 4j). Gregarious nymphs were significantly attracted to bacterial volatiles relative to the control medium (Fig. 4k). We then examined whether these volatiles promoted cannibalism using dual-choice predation assays (Fig. 4l). Two mechanically injured germ-depleted prey nymphs, matched for injury size and location, were presented simultaneously to ten starved fifth-instar gregarious predators, with one prey recolonized with E. hormaechei and the other left untreated. Predators preferentially attacked and consumed prey harbouring E. hormaechei, whereas germ-depleted controls were rarely targeted (Fig. 4m).

To identify the genetic basis of guaiacol biosynthesis, we sequenced the E. hormaechei genome and identified a cluster of three vanillic acid decarboxylase (vdc) genes, which have been previously implicated in microbial conversion of vanillic acid to guaiacol30 (Fig. 4n). Heterologous expression of this cluster in Escherichia coli (Extended Data Fig. 4d and Supplementary Fig. 1) confirmed its capacity to catalyse guaiacol production from vanillic acid in vitro (Fig. 4o). Conversely, deletion of the vdc genes in E. hormaechei (Extended Data Fig. 4e and Supplementary Fig. 1) completely abolished guaiacol production, as confirmed by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS) (Fig. 4p). These findings establish an essential role of this gene cluster in guaiacol biosynthesis.

Finally, we assessed whether microbial guaiacol biosynthesis was required for locust attraction and cannibalism. In two-choice olfactometer assays, gregarious nymphs were attracted to volatiles from wild-type E. hormaechei but not vdc-deficient mutants (Fig. 4q). Similarly, in dual-choice predation assays, starved gregarious predators preferentially attacked mechanically injured germ-depleted prey recolonized with wild-type E. hormaechei, whereas prey harbouring vdc mutants were rarely targeted despite identical injury size and location (Fig. 4r). Together, these results demonstrate that injury-associated guaiacol production by E. hormaechei is essential for converting host injury into an olfactory cue that promotes conspecific attraction and cannibalism.

Industry observers note that injured gregarious nymphs release elevated levels of guaiacol despite the increased risk of conspecific cannibalism. This raises the question of why such a seemingly costly response is maintained. We considered that guaiacol release might provide compensatory benefits to injured individuals. To explore this possibility, we first considered the antimicrobial properties of guaiacol. Previous studies have shown that guaiacol can inhibit or kill a broad range of microorganisms, including bacteria and fungi; these activities were attributed to its phenolic structure, which disrupts microbial membranes and interferes with metabolic processes31,32,33. On the basis of these properties, we proposed that guaiacol produced by E. hormaechei could provide immune benefits to injured gregarious nymphs by suppressing pathogen invasion.

It has been revealed that to test this hypothesis, we selected two pathogens commonly associated with locust mortality: intrinsic locust bacterial pathogen Proteus mirabilis34 (Extended Data Fig. 5a) and commercially available fungal insecticide Metarhizium anisopliae35 (Extended Data Fig. 5b). To determine whether guaiacol could improve resistance to pathogen invasion following injury, we used germ-depleted gregarious nymphs, which were either fed guaiacol or left untreated, and infected them with either wild-type E. hormaechei or its vdc knockout mutant (Fig. 5a). After manually injuring the nymphs, we applied infections with both M. anisopliae and P. mirabilis to the wound sites and monitored survival over several days (Fig. 5a). We found that guaiacol-fed or wild-type E. hormaechei-infected nymphs exhibited significantly higher survival rates compared with those that were non-fed or infected with the vdc-mutant E. hormaechei (Fig. 5b,c). These results indicated that guaiacol, produced by E. hormaechei, might enhance the survival of injured nymphs when exposed to pathogen infection. To confirm that this protective effect was due to the ability of guaiacol to inhibit pathogen proliferation, we quantified pathogen loads in the haemolymph of guaiacol-fed and non-fed nymphs, as well as in those infected with wild-type or vdc-mutant E. hormaechei. We observed that pathogen burdens were significantly higher in the haemolymph of non-fed and vdc-mutant-infected nymphs compared with guaiacol-fed and wild-type E. hormaechei-infected nymphs (Fig. 5d,e). These findings support the notion that guaiacol production by E. hormaechei suppresses invasion and proliferation of M. anisopliae and P. mirabilis, thereby providing immune benefits to injured locusts. Finally, to determine whether the protective effect of guaiacol-producing E. hormaechei was pathogen-specific or broadly applicable, we infected injured locusts with another opportunistic pathogen, Enterococcus faecalis34 (Extended Data Fig. 5c). As observed for P. mirabilis and M. anisopliae, guaiacol supplementation and colonization by wild-type E. hormaechei significantly suppressed pathogen infection (Extended Data Fig. 5d) and enhanced host survival (Extended Data Fig. 5e). Together, these results indicate that guaiacol functions as a broadly protective microbial metabolite that enhances host defence against diverse pathogens following injury.

PBS, phosphate-buffered saline. g, Functional annotation of differentially expressed genes; four Toll and Imd pathway genes are highlighted. h, Relative mRNA levels after guaiacol treatment (n = 3): LBP (3 h, 6 h, 9 h; P = 0.002, P = 0.004, P < 0.001), βGBP (6 h, 9 h; P = 0.030, P = 0.042), PGRP-SD (3 h, 6 h, 9 h; P = 0.003, P < 0.001, P = 0.014) and CatL (6 h, 9 h; P = 0.007, P < 0.001). i, RNAi workflow. j–l, Survival after knockdown of LBP (j; n = 80, P = 0.007), CatL (k; n = 100, P = 0.019) or βGBP (l; n = 80, P < 0.001) versus GFP controls. m, Workflow assessing immune benefits to predators consuming E. hormaechei-carrying prey. n,o, Predator survival after consumption of germ-depleted or E. hormaechei (E. h)-infected prey, followed by P. mirabilis (n; n = 100, P = 0.001) or M. anisopliae (o; n = 120, P < 0.001) infection. Data are mean ± s.d. (d, e and h). Two-sided unpaired Student’s t-tests were used, except in survival analyses (b, c, j–l, n, o; log-rank Mantel–Cox tests). ***P < 0.001; **P < 0.01; *P < 0.05. The dsGFP data presented in panels j and k are identical, as both originate from the same experiment.

To explore the mechanism underlying the suppression of pathogen proliferation, we first tested whether guaiacol directly inhibited the growth of M. anisopliae and P. mirabilis in vitro using the inhibition zone method. However, we found that both purified guaiacol and E. hormaechei failed to inhibit the growth of either pathogen (Extended Data Fig. 5f), suggesting that guaiacol does not directly suppress pathogen growth in vitro. Given this background, we proposed that the suppression of pathogen proliferation by guaiacol might instead be linked to an altered immune response in the locusts that confers enhanced pathogen resistance. In locusts, the haemolymph plays a critical part in immune defence36. To investigate the involvement of guaiacol in immune response regulation, we sequenced the transcriptomes of the haemolymph at the wound site from guaiacol-fed and non-fed germ-depleted gregarious nymphs after 3 h, 6 h and 9 h of injury (Fig. 5f). Differential gene expression analysis highlighted that substantial numbers of genes were upregulated and downregulated in the guaiacol-fed nymphs compared with the non-fed nymphs. Notably, four upregulated genes were identified in the Toll and Imd signalling pathways (Fig. 5g,h), which are known to be involved in immune defence37,38,39,40,41,42,43. These four genes, lipopolysaccharide-binding protein (LBP) and cathepsin L (CatL) have been shown to resist Gram-negative bacterial infections37,38,39, whereas β-glucan-binding protein (βGBP) has been associated with resistance to fungal infections in several insect species40,41. We proposed that in locusts, LBP and CatL might help to resist P. mirabilis infection, whereas βGBP might protect against M. anisopliae infection.

According to recent reports, to validate the roles of these genes in pathogen resistance, we used RNA interference (RNAi) (Fig. 5i) to knock down each gene individually (Extended Data Fig. 5g-i) and assessed their contributions to resistance to M. anisopliae or P. mirabilis infections. We found that knockdown of LBP and CatL (Extended Data Fig. 5g,h) promoted the invasion and proliferation of P. mirabilis (Extended Data Fig. 5j,k), leading to significantly higher mortality compared with the control GFP RNAi group (Fig. 5j,k). Knockdown of βGBP (Extended Data Fig. 5i), on the other hand, facilitated the invasion and proliferation of M. anisopliae (Extended Data Fig. 5l), also resulting in significantly higher mortality compared with the GFP RNAi control (Fig. 5l). These results indicate that guaiacol enhances resistance to P. mirabilis infection by upregulating LBP and CatL, while enhancing resistance to M. anisopliae through upregulation of βGBP. Thus, guaiacol protects injured nymphs from pathogen infection by stimulating the immune response.

As guaiacol activated immune responses in injured locusts, we next asked whether this immune activation might also restrict the proliferation of the guaiacol-producing symbiont itself. To address this possibility, we exposed germ-depleted gregarious nymphs to guaiacol or left them untreated and subsequently inoculated them with equal amounts of E. hormaechei. Under these conditions, guaiacol exposure did not reduce E. hormaechei abundance relative to untreated controls (Extended Data Fig. 5m), indicating that guaiacol-induced immune activation does not substantially impair colonization by its microbial producer. We then examined whether elevated guaiacol emission served as a direct consequence of pathogen infection. Gregarious nymphs were infected with P. mirabilis, and guaiacol emission was quantified following infection. Pathogen infection alone did not significantly alter guaiacol release compared with uninfected controls (Extended Data Fig. 5n), suggesting that elevated guaiacol production is not a general response to infection but instead is specifically associated with injury-dependent proliferation of E. hormaechei.

Having established that guaiacol neither suppresses its microbial producer nor is directly induced by pathogen infection, we next asked whether guaiacol exposure enhanced the capacity of the host to respond to subsequent pathogen challenge. Germ-depleted gregarious nymphs were fed guaiacol before localized infection of a wound site with P. mirabilis. Guaiacol treatment resulted in upregulation of multiple genes in the Toll and Imd signalling pathways, including the immune effector genes identified earlier (Extended Data Fig. 5o). These results indicate that guaiacol may enhance host immune responsiveness during subsequent bacterial infection.

Industry observers note that finally, we explored whether gregarious predator nymphs benefited from consuming injured gregarious nymphs, given that these injured nymphs host large quantities of E. hormaechei. In the experimental group, we provided germ-depleted fourth-instar gregarious nymphs infected with E. hormaechei to fifth-instar gregarious predator nymphs for feeding (Fig. 5m). In the control group, we provided germ-depleted fourth-instar gregarious nymphs without E. hormaechei infection (Fig. 5m). In both groups, we ensured that all predator nymphs consumed equal amounts of prey nymphs. We found that predators consuming E. hormaechei-infected nymphs exhibited significantly better survival when subsequently infected with pathogens, compared with those that consumed non-infected nymphs (Fig. 5n,o). To directly trace microbial transmission during cannibalism, we fed germ-depleted fifth-instar predator nymphs with prey carrying E. hormaechei (Extended Data Fig. 5p). Several days after feeding, large quantities of E. hormaechei were detected throughout the haemolymph of predator nymphs, and this was accompanied by guaiacol production (Extended Data Fig. 5q,r). By contrast, predators fed prey lacking bacteria exhibited neither E. hormaechei loads nor measurable guaiacol emission (Extended Data Fig. 5q,r). These findings demonstrate that E. hormaechei acquired through cannibalism can successfully establish in the predator haemolymph and retain its metabolic capacity to produce guaiacol following transmission.

Together, these results indicate that predator locusts may derive benefits from consuming injured nymphs, probably owing to microbial and immune support provided by the accumulated E. hormaechei.

It has been revealed that our findings demonstrate that guaiacol functions as both an internal and an external signal in gregarious locusts, acting internally to enhance immune defence while externally promoting cannibalism. This dual role probably represents an evolutionary adaptation that balances pathogen resistance with the risks of conspecific predation in response to fluctuating physiological conditions, such as injury severity. To investigate how injury severity influenced these opposing effects, we generated standardized injuries of increasing size (levels 1–6) using steel needles (Fig. 6a and Extended Data Fig. 6a). Guaiacol emissions remained low at injury levels 1–3 but increased significantly at levels 4–6 (Fig. 6b). Consistent with this pattern, starved gregarious predators indicated no preference between intact and injured prey at levels 1–3 but preferentially attacked injured nymphs at levels 4–6 (Fig. 6a,c). The latter injuries approximated those caused by hind-tarsus loss or bites from fifth-instar locusts (Extended Data Fig. 6a). Prey movement distance and speed did not differ significantly across injury levels (Extended Data Fig. 6b,c); this enabled us to exclude differences in mobility as an explanation for predation preferences. These results indicate that elevated guaiacol emission associated with severe injury promotes cannibalistic attacks.

The two types of prey were immobilized at opposite ends of the arena. d, Workflow assessing the effects of injury size on survival following PBS or pathogen treatment. e,f, Survival following PBS or infection with P. mirabilis (e; level 4, P < 0.001; levels 5 and 6, P < 0.001) or M. anisopliae (f; level 3, P = 0.015; level 4, P < 0.001; levels 5 and 6, P < 0.001), quantified at 3 days and 5 days, respectively (n = 6 replicates per group; 10 nymphs per replicate). g, Workflow to assess survival of germ-depleted nymphs inoculated with wild-type or vdc-mutant E. hormaechei before PBS or pathogen treatment. h,i, Survival following PBS injection or infection with P. mirabilis (h; level 1, P = 0.003; level 2, P = 0.016; level 3, P = 0.010) or M. anisopliae (i; levels 1 and 2, P < 0.001; level 3, P = 0.005) (n = 6 replicates per group; 10 nymphs per replicate).
